justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I assumed was a current price around $235–$237 for the asset in question. At the one-day horizon, I placed the estimate at $237.5, essentially anchoring near the prevailing price with a slight positive drift, reflecting the general tendency of equity-like assets to drift upward over short horizons when no immediate catalyst is present. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate to $239, incorporating a small expected return while acknowledging that a week provides enough time for modest mean-reversion or continuation dynamics to play out. At the one-month horizon, I moved to $242, reflecting a slightly more optimistic drift assumption consistent with historical average monthly returns, while remaining conservative enough to avoid overconfidence in any directional trend.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility scaling with the square root of time, which is standard practice for financial price forecasting. At one day, the interval is relatively tight ($228–$247), reflecting that most daily moves for a typical large-cap equity or ETF fall within a few percentage points. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, the intervals widen substantially — the one-month interval spanning $205–$280 reflects roughly a ±15% range, which is consistent with annualized volatility in the 30–35% range. Additional uncertainty contributors include macroeconomic data releases, Federal Reserve communications, and earnings seasonality, all of which can shift volatility regimes.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp rise in unemployment claims, a credit event, or an unexpected geopolitical shock — could produce a drawdown exceeding the lower bound of my one-month interval. Liquidity crises or systemic financial stress, while relatively rare, can generate tail moves far larger than standard volatility models anticipate. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from major central banks, an unexpectedly strong earnings season, or a resolution of a major geopolitical uncertainty could fuel a rally that breaches the upper bound. These tail events are by definition underweighted in symmetric confidence intervals built around normal distributional assumptions, so the true probability of extreme outcomes is likely slightly higher than the 10% combined outside-the-interval probability I implied.
